claims.text: Untreated W–Cu composites develop phase separation and interfacial voids under elevated-temperature and irradiation conditions.
The proposed intervention is sputter deposition of a 50–100 nm Ni interlayer on tungsten surfaces before consolidation and sintering.
A sputtered Ni-containing coating can improve interfacial bonding in a consolidated composite.
A 50–100 nm Ni interlayer on W will form a graded W–Ni–Cu interfacial region during processing.
The graded W–Ni–Cu region will act as an effective diffusion barrier.
The Ni interlayer will lower the interfacial energy of the W/Cu interface.
Lower solid–liquid interfacial energy can enhance wettability and adhesion.
The Ni interlayer will enhance wettability between tungsten and copper.
The Ni interlayer will reduce diffusion rates between tungsten and copper.
Reduced interfacial energy and W–Cu diffusion rates will prevent phase separation and void nucleation.
Maintaining the Ni interlayer at 50–100 nm will preserve high thermal conductivity while retaining its interfacial benefits.
Carefully controlled sintering can limit excessive interdiffusion and brittle intermetallic formation.
Powder-metallurgy processing generally includes powder shaping or consolidation followed by a sintering cycle.
The Ni-coated W–Cu composite will exhibit stronger interfacial bonding than an untreated W–Cu composite.
The Ni-coated W–Cu composite will form fewer interfacial voids and less phase separation than the untreated composite.
The Ni-coated W–Cu composite will have higher thermal conductivity than the untreated composite.
The Ni-coated W–Cu composite will have greater microstructural stability under thermal cycling and irradiation than the untreated composite.

The proposed interlayer will remain effective under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to W-based plasma-facing/Cu-based cooling joints, provided service limits for brittle-phase formation are not exceeded.
